name: Why Not?
tagline: There's an easier way. It just isn't as much fun.
epigraph: Taverns heated drinks like this with a red-hot iron. This one burns its sugar instead.
glassware: a wide china teacup (about 200 ml), warmed with hot water first
language_row: Wren's Resonance on reading v4: ready. As the guest, "you could just buy one" is the sentence, and the gift line lets them feel valued for the thing they're teased about. Barnum watch: "it lit you up" is held by the scene and the cage line. Sibling swap clean: *For Good* (annoyance, a fix that disappears), *Nothing to It* (looks easy; this one looks hard on purpose), *In a Minute*. Collisions resolved: "sensible" stays *The Other Berry*'s (the cage here is "you could just buy one"); "You made it." (*For Good*) → "you both built it"; five stock-phrase 4-grams swapped. whoYouAre cut from 200 to 164 words. Pronoun warnings accepted by Wren: "he" in yours 2–4 is Arnold, never the guest. ✓
sources: Studio fact card `_studio/fact-cards/dave-arnold-red-hot-poker.md` (Dave Arnold, *Liquid Intelligence* pp. 45, 48, 177–191, his words; Robert Simonson, *A Proper Drink* pp. 223–226; *Oxford Companion* FLIP pdf 812–813, LOGGERHEAD pdf 1189; David Wondrich, *Imbibe!* pdf 126). Drink: *Liquid Intelligence* p. 184 (the faux-poker: sugar burned in a pan) and p. 187 (Red-Hot Ale); *Flavor Matrix* caramel pdf 72 (molasses as caramel's substitute; toasted, roasted flavours as it darkens). Set aside: William "the Only William" Schmidt (*Imbibe!* pdf 56–57; the plan's lead, overturned in round 1). Room notes: `work/explorer-jester/`.
names_note: **Why Not?**, the room's pick (all three): the person's whole reason, and the drink is the joke in it (why not just pour the syrup?); the story's "why not?" is Simonson's portrait of Arnold, attributed, so the title puts no words in his mouth. Runner-up: **Something Crucial** (Arnold's phrase for what the pot lost, *LI* p. 177; it may spend y1's line twice). Also considered: *Pan Style* (Arnold's own label), *The Long Way Round* (leans on the tagline).
open_items: **The plan's lead was overturned (round 1):** Wren read *Imbibe!* pdf 56–57 whole and found Schmidt's motive on the page is impressing the guest ("likes to impress you with the idea that he is taking a great deal of trouble on your account"), which is showmanship, not tinkering. Schmidt is released to other families (note in `plans/explorer.md`).

**Arnold is also *Overnight*'s person** (creator-magician, the milk wash). Owned here, not in the guest's text: *Overnight* is a method that looked like a mistake and came out better; this one is the long way chosen on purpose, with the easy way sitting right there. The reading never says "mistake", "didn't mean" or "surprise".

**No poker at home, no flame (Tomás, Hester):** Arnold won't sell or describe his electric pokers, and his home soldering copper can make drinks "taste like you are sucking on a penny". His faux-poker flambés the liquor after burning the sugar; ours drops the flame (fire and an audience are *The Entertainer*'s ground), so the drink is ours "after his", never his recipe. The rum goes in off the heat.

**Contains gluten (abbey ale):** the iron toasted the grain (Oxford pdf 813), so the ale is the base the story worked on; cider is period-true too (Oxford pdf 812) and was swept in range, but Tomás ruled ale and Wren conceded. This pour leaves the veto-free floor; its five closed siblings are veto-free.

**Kept from *Nothing to It*:** that pour takes white sugar off at amber for a cold Old-Fashioned and its closing line is about when to stop; here the sugar is burned dark in a pan as part of a hot drink, and no word says "amber", "close" or anything about the edge of burning. Muscovado (Morse's 1792 flip) was declined by Tomás: it starts dark and hides the one judgement the method rests on.

**Fences on the story (Hester):** the rotovap Arnold *bought* is out (it argues against "you could just buy one"); "why not?" and the railroad penny are Simonson's portrait, attributed; the bar is dated (opened with David Chang in 2012) and told in the past tense; he didn't invent the poker (the colonial innkeepers' iron, brought back); the flip's sea origin is left out; "Not many bars followed his example" (*Proper* p. 226) is why the reading never says people rushed to copy him.

**Bottle ranges (Tomás's sweep):** ale at 6–8% and rum at 40–43% (a 9% ale with 46% rum goes OUT at 14.0%); 9 g of sugar if the ale tastes sweet. Ale sugar and acid set at nil as in Arnold's Red-Hot Ale stats; at plain-beer table values the acid edges over, and the lemon is what goes.
